title: Job 38 — YHWH from the whirlwind: the cosmological challenge

paragraphs.text: וַיַּֽעַן־יְהוָ֣ה אֶת־אִ֭יּוֹב מנ הסערה [מִ֥ן ׀] [הַסְּעָרָ֗ה] וַיֹּאמַֽר׃

i18n.en: Then YHWH answered Job from the whirlwind, and said:

paragraphs.commentary: **The voice comes from the whirlwind.** *Min ha-se'arah* — *from the whirlwind/storm*. The noun *se'arah* (סְעָרָה) is the same word that opened Ezekiel's vision at Ezek 1:4 — *ruach se'arah ba'ah min ha-tzafon* — *a stormy wind coming from the north*. The chapter is staging YHWH's voice in the same meteorological-vehicular register as Ezekiel's chayyot-throne apparatus. // The verb *vayya'an* — *answered* — frames the speech as a *response*, not an unprompted address. The 35 chapters of preceding dialogue (Job's complaints, the friends' arguments, Elihu's interventions) constitute the question; YHWH's answer arrives in the storm. // *Ketiv/qere* note: the text has *mn ha-se'arah* as ketiv with the Masoretic vocalization breaking it into *min* + *ha-se'arah* as qere. The qere reading is straightforward; the ketiv may reflect a less-standard spelling. The translation uses the qere.

paragraphs.text: מִ֤י זֶ֨ה ׀ מַחְשִׁ֖יךְ עֵצָ֥ה בְמִלִּ֗ין בְּֽלִי־דָֽעַת׃

i18n.en: Who is this who darkens counsel with words without knowledge?

paragraphs.commentary: **The opening rebuke.** *Machshikh etzah* — *darkening counsel*. The verb *chashakh* (darken, obscure) is the Hebrew Bible's standard term for the bringing-of-darkness — same root as *choshekh* (darkness) of Gen 1:2. *Etzah* is *counsel, plan, deliberative wisdom*. // The challenge is rhetorical: who is the person obscuring *counsel* (the divine deliberative plan) with *words without knowledge*? The implied answer: Job — and by extension all his speakers. The 35 chapters of dialogue have been *darkening* the divine plan with insufficient information.

paragraphs.text: אֱזָר־נָ֣א כְגֶ֣בֶר חֲלָצֶ֑יךָ וְ֝אֶשְׁאָלְךָ֗ וְהוֹדִיעֵֽנִי׃

i18n.en: Gird up your loins like a strong man — I will question you, and you instruct me.

paragraphs.commentary: **The challenge-form.** *Ezar-na khe-gever chalatzekha* — *gird up your loins like a strong man*. The verb *azar* (gird, belt up) names the act of preparing for combat or physical labor; *gever* is *strong man, warrior* (not just *adam* — *human* — but the warrior-specific noun). // The verb-sequence (*esha'alekha v'hodi'eni* — *I will ask you and you instruct me*) inverts the dialogue's prior direction. Job has been demanding YHWH's reply for 35 chapters; YHWH now reframes: *you* take the questioning position; *I* will inform you. The chapter is staging the reversal of the dialogue's address-direction.

paragraphs.text: אֵיפֹ֣ה הָ֭יִיתָ בְּיָסְדִי־אָ֑רֶץ הַ֝גֵּ֗ד אִם־יָדַ֥עְתָּ בִינָֽה׃

i18n.en: Where were you when I founded the earth? Tell — if you know understanding.

paragraphs.commentary: **The cosmological-temporal challenge.** *Eyfo hayita b'yosdi-aretz* — *where were you when I founded the earth*. The verb *yasad* (found, lay the foundation of) is the architectural-construction term; the chapter is invoking the canonical Hebrew Bible image of the earth as a built-structure (cf. Ps 24:2, Ps 102:25, Isa 48:13). // The challenge sets the chapter's structural premise: Job (and humans generally) were not present at the cosmological founding. The chapter will catalog the things-Job-was-not-present-for as the substance of YHWH's answer. The 'where were you' question is the chapter's keystone interrogative — it will recur in implicit form across the catalog.

paragraphs.text: מִי־שָׂ֣ם מְ֭מַדֶּיהָ כִּ֣י תֵדָ֑ע א֤וֹ מִֽי־נָטָ֖ה עָלֶ֣יהָ קָּֽו׃

i18n.en: Who set its measurements — for you must know — or who stretched the measuring line over it?

paragraphs.commentary: **Architectural-measurement vocabulary.** *Memaddeyha* — *its measurements / dimensions*. *Qav* — *measuring line, plumb line*. The chapter is invoking the toolkit of an *architect* / *builder*: someone who *measures the dimensions* and *stretches the line* over a site before construction. The chapter is staging YHWH-as-cosmic-architect, in technically-specified construction vocabulary.

paragraphs.text: עַל־מָ֭ה אֲדָנֶ֣יהָ הָטְבָּ֑עוּ א֥וֹ מִֽי־יָ֝רָ֗ה אֶ֣בֶן פִּנָּתָֽהּ׃

i18n.en: On what were its bases sunk, or who laid its cornerstone —

paragraphs.commentary: **Foundation-imagery continues.** *Adaneha* (*its bases*) — the same word used for the bases of the Tabernacle pillars (Ex 26:19, etc.) — pedestals sunk into the ground. *Even pinnatah* — *its cornerstone* — the architectural-symbolic foundation-stone. // The chapter is naming the earth's foundation as a *sunk-pedestal-and-cornerstone* construction. The reading is technical-architectural, not metaphorical-vague. Whether this is meant as cosmological-mythopoetic (the earth resting on cosmic pillars in ANE cosmology) or as procedural-construction language (the earth founded *as if* on architectural pedestals) is part of the chapter's ambiguity. The translation preserves both possibilities.

paragraphs.text: בְּרָן־יַ֭חַד כּ֣וֹכְבֵי בֹ֑קֶר וַ֝יָּרִ֗יעוּ כָּל־בְּנֵ֥י אֱלֹהִֽים׃

i18n.en: when the morning stars sang together and all the sons of the Elohim shouted for joy?

paragraphs.commentary: **The third Hebrew Bible bnei-elohim attestation.** ***Kol bnei Elohim va-yariyu*** — *all the sons of the Elohim shouted for joy*. The chapter places the *bnei elohim* — the divine-council class introduced in Gen 6:2-4 (the *bnei ha-elohim* who took daughters of the human as wives) and re-deployed in Job 1:6, 2:1 (the *bnei ha-elohim* presenting themselves before YHWH) — at the **moment of cosmic founding**. This is the third Hebrew Bible explicit attestation of the class. // *Kokhvei voqer* — *morning stars* — are placed in parallel with the *bnei elohim*. The two phrases form a poetic couplet, and the parallel reading identifies them: the *morning stars sang* / *the bnei elohim shouted*. The same beings are named in two registers — astronomical (*stars*) and divine-council (*bnei elohim*). // The lens reads this parallel with attention: the chapter is identifying the *bnei elohim* with celestial bodies / celestial-beings at the founding of the earth. The same identification recurs in later Hebrew Bible literature (Isa 14:13 'the stars of El', Dan 8:10 'the host of the heavens'); the LXX of Deut 32:8 reads *bnei elohim* where the Masoretic Text has *bnei Yisrael* — at minimum, the text-historical tradition preserves the *bnei elohim*-as-celestial-class reading. // The verb *va-yariyu* (hifil of *rua* — *shout, raise a war-cry, sound an alarm*) is military-celebratory. The bnei elohim are *shouting* at the cosmic founding — an organized choral acclamation.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֣סֶךְ בִּדְלָתַ֣יִם יָ֑ם בְּ֝גִיח֗וֹ מֵרֶ֥חֶם יֵצֵֽא׃

i18n.en: Or who shut up the sea with doors when it burst forth, came out of the womb?

paragraphs.commentary: **Sea-cosmogony.** The chapter is reusing the Hebrew Bible / ANE cosmogonic image of the *sea-restraint*: a primordial chaos-sea that has to be *shut behind doors* to contain it. The image matches the Mesopotamian Tiamat-restraint tradition and Genesis 1:9-10's *gathering the waters* / *creating the dry land*. // *B'gicho me-rechem yetze* — *when it burst forth, came out of the womb*. The chapter is using birth-imagery: the sea is born from a womb. The image personalizes the cosmic-restraint procedure: the sea is not just a mass of water but a creaturely-emerging entity that had to be *delivered* and then *contained*. // The lens reads the chapter's combined-architectural-and-birth imagery: the cosmos is being built (vv 4-6) and the chaos is being birthed-and-contained (vv 8-11). Both vocabularies operate together.

paragraphs.text: בְּשׂוּמִ֣י עָנָ֣ן לְבֻשׁ֑וֹ וַ֝עֲרָפֶ֗ל חֲתֻלָּתֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: when I made the cloud its garment, and thick darkness its swaddling band,

paragraphs.commentary: **The sea's birth-clothing.** *Anan l'vusho* — *the cloud as its garment*. *Arafel chatulato* — *thick darkness as its swaddling band* (*chatulah* — *swaddling cloth* — is a hapax, but transparent from *chatal*, a verb related to wrapping). // The chapter continues the birth-imagery: as a newborn is *swaddled*, the new-born sea is *swaddled in cloud and darkness*. The image is striking — the chaos-waters are *wrapped*, *clothed*, *contained* in the same way an infant is wrapped at birth.

paragraphs.text: וָאֶשְׁבֹּ֣ר עָלָ֣יו חֻקִּ֑י וָֽ֝אָשִׂ֗ים בְּרִ֣יחַ וּדְלָתָֽיִם׃

i18n.en: and I broke my boundary over it and set a bar and doors;

paragraphs.commentary: ***Eshbor alav chuqqi*** — *I broke my boundary over it*. The verb *shavar* (break) is unusual here; the standard cognate-construction would be *sim chok* (set a boundary). The chapter uses *broke my boundary on it* — possibly a hapax-style construction meaning *imposed* the boundary by *breaking it through* the unbounded sea. // *Beriach u-dlatayim* — *a bar and doors* — names the gate-and-bolt of containment. The image: the sea is *behind a barred gate*.

paragraphs.text: וָאֹמַ֗ר עַד־פֹּ֣ה תָ֭בוֹא וְלֹ֣א תֹסִ֑יף וּפֹ֥א־יָ֝שִׁ֗ית בִּגְא֥וֹן גַּלֶּֽיךָ׃

i18n.en: and I said, "This far you shall come and no further, and here shall the pride of your waves be stayed."

paragraphs.commentary: ***Ad-po tavo v-lo tosif*** — *this far you shall come and no further*. The chapter completes the sea-restraint with a direct quotation of YHWH's commanding word. The phrase is one of the Hebrew Bible's most-quoted boundary-setting formulas. // *G'on galekha* — *the pride of your waves*. *Ga'on* (pride, exaltation, majesty) is the chapter's personalizing register: the waves have *pride*. The chaos-sea is treated as a creaturely entity capable of *pridefulness* that has to be put-in-its-place by command.

paragraphs.text: הְֽ֭מִיָּמֶיךָ צִוִּ֣יתָ בֹּ֑קֶר ידעתה שחר [יִדַּ֖עְתָּה] [הַשַּׁ֣חַר] מְקֹמֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: Have you ever in your days commanded the morning, or caused the dawn to know its place,

paragraphs.commentary: **The challenge shifts to daily-cyclic phenomena.** The chapter pivots from cosmogonic foundation-events to recurring atmospheric phenomena. The morning, the dawn, the day-night cycle. The interrogative *ha-mi-yamekha* — *have you ever in your days* — frames the question in terms of *recurring cosmic management*, not just origins. // *Ketiv/qere* note: *yedaeta ha-shachar* (qere) for *yidatah shachar* (ketiv). The qere is the standard reading: 'have you caused the dawn to know'.

paragraphs.text: לֶ֭אֱחֹז בְּכַנְפ֣וֹת הָאָ֑רֶץ וְיִנָּעֲר֖וּ רְשָׁעִ֣ים מִמֶּֽנָּה׃

i18n.en: to take hold of the wings of the land, that the wicked may be shaken out of it?

paragraphs.commentary: **The morning as a corrective-mechanism.** *Le'echoz b'kanfot ha-aretz* — *to take hold of the wings of the land*. The image: dawn *grabs the corners of the earth* (literally *wings* — same word as in bird-wings or garment-corners) and *shakes out* the wicked. The wicked who hid under cover of night are exposed at daybreak. The chapter is staging the day-night cycle as a *judicial mechanism* — the daily-dawn function is to *expose wrongdoing*.

paragraphs.text: תִּ֭תְהַפֵּךְ כְּחֹ֣מֶר חוֹתָ֑ם וְ֝יִֽתְיַצְּב֗וּ כְּמ֣וֹ לְבֽוּשׁ׃

i18n.en: It is changed like clay under a seal, and they stand out like a garment.

paragraphs.commentary: **Two technological images.** *K'chomer chotam* — *like clay under a seal*. The image is the cylinder-seal pressed into clay (Mesopotamian sealing-practice) — the earth as a clay surface that receives the morning's *imprint*, producing a pattern. *Yityatzvu k'mo l'vush* — *they stand out like a garment* — the night's hidden features become *visible* as morning dresses the land. // Both images are technical-craft (seal-making, weaving). The chapter is staging the daily-dawn as a *craft-procedural* event.

paragraphs.text: וְיִמָּנַ֣ע מֵרְשָׁעִ֣ים אוֹרָ֑ם וּזְר֥וֹעַ רָ֝מָ֗ה תִּשָּׁבֵֽר׃

i18n.en: Their light is withheld from the wicked, and the uplifted arm is broken.

paragraphs.text: הֲ֭בָאתָ עַד־נִבְכֵי־יָ֑ם וּבְחֵ֥קֶר תְּ֝ה֗וֹם הִתְהַלָּֽכְתָּ׃

i18n.en: Have you come to the springs of the sea, or walked in the searching of the deep?

paragraphs.commentary: **The deep-investigation challenge.** *Nivkhei yam* — *springs of the sea* — *nevekh* (נֵבֶךְ) is a hapax, but probably means *deep-source, abyssal-spring*. The chapter is naming the **deep submarine source-points** of the sea, not the surface. *Cheker tehom* — *the searching/probing of the deep*. *Cheker* (חֵקֶר) is *investigation, search* — a deliberate exploratory verb. // The question is whether Job has *been to* the deep submarine sources — has he done the **deep-sea exploration**? *Tehom* is the same word as in Gen 1:2 — the primordial deep, etymologically cognate with Akkadian *tiāmtu*/Tiamat (cf. glossary entry `tehom`). // The lens reads this with interest: the chapter is staging the deep submarine domain as a place that *requires investigation* — that has *springs* (specific source-points) and that allows *walking-about* in its *searching*. The image is exploratory-investigative.

paragraphs.text: הֲנִגְל֣וּ לְ֭ךָ שַׁעֲרֵי־מָ֑וֶת וְשַׁעֲרֵ֖י צַלְמָ֣וֶת תִּרְאֶֽה׃

i18n.en: Have the gates of death been revealed to you, or have you seen the gates of deep darkness?

paragraphs.commentary: **Death-domain challenge.** *Sha'arei mavet v-sha'arei tzalmavet* — *gates of death and gates of deep darkness*. // *Sha'arei mavet* recurs in Hebrew Bible at Ps 9:14, 107:18 — gates of the realm-of-the-dead. *Tzalmavet* (צַלְמָוֶת) is variously analyzed: *shadow of death* (the traditional reading, *tzel + mavet*) or *deep darkness* (modern reading, from a root *tzalam* meaning 'be very dark'). The combined image: there are *gates* into the death-domain, with their own architecture and access-controls. // The chapter is staging the death-domain as a *bounded territory with entry-gates* — not as a generic dissolution. The reading-question Job is being asked: have you accessed these gates? Have you seen them?

paragraphs.text: הִ֭תְבֹּנַנְתָּ עַד־רַחֲבֵי־אָ֑רֶץ הַ֝גֵּ֗ד אִם־יָדַ֥עְתָּ כֻלָּֽהּ׃

i18n.en: Have you considered the breadth of the land? Tell — if you know all of it.

paragraphs.text: אֵי־זֶ֣ה הַ֭דֶּרֶךְ יִשְׁכָּן־א֑וֹר וְ֝חֹ֗שֶׁךְ אֵי־זֶ֥ה מְקֹמֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: Where is the way to where the light dwells, and darkness — where is its place?

paragraphs.text: כִּ֣י תִ֭קָּחֶנּוּ אֶל־גְּבוּל֑וֹ וְכִֽי־תָ֝בִ֗ין נְתִיב֥וֹת בֵּיתֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: that you might take it to its boundary, that you might understand the paths to its house?

paragraphs.commentary: **Light and darkness as locations.** Vv 19-20 stage *light* and *darkness* as **places-with-dwellings**: each has a *way*, a *house*, *paths*, *boundaries*. The chapter is treating the light-dark cycle as a *commuting* phenomenon — light dwells somewhere and travels from there; darkness has its own residence. // The poetic-cosmological image — *light dwells*, *darkness has its place* — matches the Hebrew Bible's broader cosmology where day and night are quasi-personalized entities with locations (cf. Ps 19:5, where the sun has a *tent* it leaves from each morning). // The challenge: does Job know the *paths to the house of light*? The answer is plainly no — the chapter is exposing the limit of human-positional knowledge.

paragraphs.text: יָ֭דַעְתָּ כִּי־אָ֣ז תִּוָּלֵ֑ד וּמִסְפַּ֖ר יָמֶ֣יךָ רַבִּֽים׃

i18n.en: You know — for then you were born, and the number of your days is great.

paragraphs.commentary: **Ironic concession.** The verse is read sarcastically: *you know, of course, because you were born back then* (i.e., at the cosmic founding) *and your days are many* (i.e., as long as the cosmos). The chapter is mocking the implicit-presumption of Job's prior speeches: the human-temporal scale is being thrown into relief against the cosmic-temporal scale.

paragraphs.text: הֲ֭בָאתָ אֶל־אֹצְר֣וֹת שָׁ֑לֶג וְאֹצְר֖וֹת בָּרָ֣ד תִּרְאֶֽה׃

i18n.en: Have you entered the storehouses of snow, or seen the storehouses of hail —

paragraphs.commentary: **The weather-storehouses.** *Otzrot sheleg v-otzrot barad* — *storehouses of snow and storehouses of hail*. The Hebrew noun *otzar* (אוֹצָר) is the standard term for a **storehouse, treasury, armory** — Joseph's grain-storehouses (Gen 41:56), the Temple-treasures (1 Kgs 7:51), military arsenals (Jer 50:25). // The image is striking: weather phenomena (snow, hail) are stored in *storehouses* — physical containers that hold them until they are released. The next verse will name the *release-purpose*: trouble, war.

paragraphs.text: אֲשֶׁר־חָשַׂ֥כְתִּי לְעֶת־צָ֑ר לְי֥וֹם קְ֝רָ֗ב וּמִלְחָמָֽה׃

i18n.en: which I have reserved for the time of distress, for the day of battle and war?

paragraphs.commentary: **The storehouses as armory.** *Chasakhti l-et tzar l-yom q'rav u-milchamah* — *I have reserved for the time of distress, for the day of battle and war*. The chapter is naming the weather-storehouses as **military reserves** — snow and hail are *strategic weapons* deployed at specified times. // The reading is consistent with broader Hebrew Bible weather-as-divine-weapon imagery: hail in Josh 10:11 (the Amorite-coalition defeat), Ex 9:18-26 (the seventh Egyptian plague), Ezek 13:11-13, 38:22 (eschatological judgment hailstorms). The chapter is staging the weather-system as a *deployable arsenal*.

paragraphs.text: אֵי־זֶ֣ה הַ֭דֶּרֶךְ יֵחָ֣לֶק א֑וֹר יָפֵ֖ץ קָדִ֣ים עֲלֵי־אָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: Where is the way the light is divided, the east wind scattered upon the earth?

paragraphs.text: מִֽי־פִלַּ֣ג לַשֶּׁ֣טֶף תְּעָלָ֑ה וְ֝דֶ֗רֶךְ לַחֲזִ֥יז קֹלֽוֹת׃

i18n.en: Who cleft a channel for the flood, and a way for the thunderstorm,

paragraphs.commentary: **Atmospheric-channel imagery.** *T'alah la-sheteph* — *a channel for the flood*. *Derekh la-chaziz qolot* — *a way for the thunderstorm*. The chapter is staging atmospheric phenomena as **routed via designed channels**: flood-water has its specified channel; thunderstorms have their specified pathways. The image is canal-system / waterworks engineering applied to the atmosphere.

paragraphs.text: לְ֭הַמְטִיר עַל־אֶ֣רֶץ לֹא־אִ֑ישׁ מִ֝דְבָּ֗ר לֹא־אָדָ֥ם בּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: to cause rain to fall on the land — no one there — the desert with no human in it,

paragraphs.text: לְהַשְׂבִּ֣יעַ שֹׁ֭אָה וּמְשֹׁאָ֑ה וּ֝לְהַצְמִ֗יחַ מֹ֣צָא דֶֽשֶׁא׃

i18n.en: to saturate desolate wasteland and cause the growth of vegetation to sprout?

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter's quiet aside.** Rain falls on the desert where no human lives. The chapter is noting that the divine weather-system operates **independently of human benefit** — rain goes where no human is, watering *desolate wasteland* and bringing forth vegetation that no human will harvest. The cosmic-management runs on its own terms, not on terms of human-utility.

paragraphs.text: הֲיֵשׁ־לַמָּטָ֥ר אָ֑ב א֥וֹ מִי־ה֝וֹלִ֗יד אֶגְלֵי־טָֽל׃

i18n.en: Does the rain have a father, or who fathered the drops of dew?

paragraphs.commentary: **Birth-imagery for atmospheric phenomena.** The chapter continues the *cosmic birth* register from vv 8-9: now rain and dew are *fathered* / *birthed*. The image is generative-genealogical: weather phenomena have *parents*, *originators*.

paragraphs.text: מִבֶּ֣טֶן מִ֭י יָצָ֣א הַקָּ֑רַח וּכְפֹ֥ר שָׁ֝מַיִם מִ֣י יְלָדֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: From whose womb came the ice, and the frost of the skies — who bore it?

paragraphs.text: כָּ֭אֶבֶן מַ֣יִם יִתְחַבָּ֑אוּ וּפְנֵ֥י תְ֝ה֗וֹם יִתְלַכָּֽדוּ׃

i18n.en: The waters become hidden like stone, and the face of the deep is captured.

paragraphs.commentary: **Freezing imagery.** *Ka-even mayim yitchabba'u* — *the waters become hidden like stone*. *P'nei tehom yitlakkadu* — *the face of the deep is captured/seized*. The chapter is describing the **freezing of water-surfaces** in technical language: water becoming stone-like (ice), the deep being *captured* / *gripped* (frozen). // Verbs are precise: *chava* (be hidden, withdraw) names the transformation of liquid to solid as a *hiding* — the liquid waters hidden inside their own frozen surface. *Lakhad* (capture, seize) names the freezing of the deep as a *capture-event*.

paragraphs.text: הַֽ֭תְקַשֵּׁר מַעֲדַנּ֣וֹת כִּימָ֑ה אֽוֹ־מֹשְׁכ֖וֹת כְּסִ֣יל תְּפַתֵּֽחַ׃

i18n.en: Can you bind the chains of Kimah, or loose the cords of Kesil?

paragraphs.commentary: **The constellations enter.** *Kimah* (כִּימָה) is generally identified with **the Pleiades** (the seven sister-stars in Taurus); *Kesil* (כְּסִיל) with **Orion** (the canonical hunter-constellation). The same pair appears in Job 9:9 and Amos 5:8. // The image-language is specific: *ma'adannot Kimah* — *the chains of Kimah* (Pleiades bound in cluster-formation); *mosh'khot Kesil* — *the cords of Kesil* (Orion held by his belt-and-bands). The chapter is reading the constellations as **physically-restrained patterns** — bound into their formations by cosmic ropes / chains. The challenge: can Job *bind* or *loose* these cosmic-tied configurations? // The lens reads this verse with strong interest. The Wheel of Heaven framework engages the precession-of-the-equinoxes and the cosmic-clock astronomy as a load-bearing element of the project's cosmology. Job 38:31 is one of the Hebrew Bible's most explicit named-constellation references — the chapter has the canonical Hebrew Bible vocabulary for the Pleiades-Orion cluster, which the precession-of-the-equinoxes calculations have used as reference-stars for millennia. The chapter's stated challenge (can you bind/loose these?) acknowledges the constellations as **fixed-cycle astronomical structures** whose timing and configuration are not subject to human manipulation.

paragraphs.text: הֲתֹצִ֣יא מַזָּר֣וֹת בְּעִתּ֑וֹ וְ֝עַ֗יִשׁ עַל־בָּנֶ֥יהָ תַנְחֵֽם׃

i18n.en: Can you bring forth the Mazzaroth in its appointed time, or guide Ayish with her children?

paragraphs.commentary: **Two more astronomical-class names.** *Mazzarot* (מַזָּרוֹת) is a hapax (occurring only here). The traditional identification (LXX, Vulgate) is **the zodiac constellations** — the twelve constellations of the ecliptic through which the sun, moon, and planets appear to move. The word may be cognate with Akkadian *manzaltu* (a celestial-position term) or with the Hebrew root *zarah* (scatter — possibly the scattered band of zodiacal constellations). The Mishnaic Hebrew *mazzal* (mazzaltot in plural — *fortune-stars*) descends from this term. // *Be-ito* — *in its appointed time* — names the **timed cycle**: the zodiac is brought-forth on schedule, in the precise calendrical rhythm. // *Ayish* (עַיִשׁ) — *the Bear constellation* — is generally identified with **Ursa Major (the Great Bear)**, also called *Ash* (עָשׁ) at Job 9:9. *Bnei Ayish* — *the children of Ayish* — names the cluster of stars forming the Bear-constellation. // The four named celestial objects of vv 31-32 (Kimah/Pleiades, Kesil/Orion, Mazzarot/Zodiac, Ayish/Bear) are the canonical Hebrew Bible **astronomical-reference catalogue**. The chapter is staging Job's confrontation with **timed-cyclical cosmic astronomy** as something he plainly does not control. // For the WoH framework specifically: the Mazzarot timing-cycle is the chapter's most direct invocation of the **calendrical-zodiacal** astronomy that the precession-of-the-equinoxes framework operates within. The Hebrew text has, in this verse, the technical vocabulary for the cosmic-clock the Wheel of Heaven engages.

paragraphs.text: הֲ֭יָדַעְתָּ חֻקּ֣וֹת שָׁמָ֑יִם אִם־תָּשִׂ֖ים מִשְׁטָר֣וֹ בָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: Do you know the ordinances of the skies? Can you set its dominion on the land?

paragraphs.commentary: ***Chuqot shamayim*** — *ordinances of the skies*. The compound names **fixed cosmic laws / regulations** governing the heavens. *Chuqot* (חֻקּוֹת) is the plural of *choq* — *statute, ordinance, prescribed rule*. The chapter is asserting that the heavens operate under **prescribed law-like regularity** — *chuqot*, statutes, not random behavior. // The compound *chuqot shamayim* recurs in Jer 33:25 (YHWH's covenant with day and night, *chuqot shamayim va-aretz* — *the ordinances of the heavens and the earth*). The chapter's framing is consistent with the broader Hebrew Bible cosmological vocabulary: cosmic operations are **lawful**, predictable, calendrically-tracked. // *Mishtaro ba-aretz* — *its dominion on the land*. *Mishtar* (משׁטר) is a hapax-style noun from the root *shatar* (rule, govern). The image: the skies *govern* the earth via their ordinances. The astrological-influence model is implicit — what happens in the heavens *rules* what happens on the land. The chapter is engaging the broader ANE astrological-cosmological framework directly.

paragraphs.text: הֲתָרִ֣ים לָעָ֣ב קוֹלֶ֑ךָ וְֽשִׁפְעַת־מַ֥יִם תְּכַסֶּֽךָּ׃

i18n.en: Can you lift up your voice to the cloud — that abundance of water cover you?

paragraphs.text: הַֽתְשַׁלַּ֣ח בְּרָקִ֣ים וְיֵלֵ֑כוּ וְיֹאמְר֖וּ לְךָ֣ הִנֵּֽנוּ׃

i18n.en: Can you send out lightnings, that they go and say to you, "Here we are"?

paragraphs.commentary: **Lightnings respond to direct command.** *Vayoremu lekha hinnenu* — *and they say to you, 'here we are'*. The personifying touch is striking: the lightnings *speak*, responding to dispatch with the standard Hebrew Bible report-formula *hinneni / hinnenu* (here I am / here we are) — the same formula Moses and Samuel and Isaiah use when YHWH calls them (Ex 3:4, 1 Sam 3:4-8, Isa 6:8). The chapter is staging lightning-bolts as *responsive subordinates* — sent on mission, reporting in.

paragraphs.text: מִי־שָׁ֭ת בַּטֻּח֣וֹת חָכְמָ֑ה א֤וֹ מִֽי־נָתַ֖ן לַשֶּׂ֣כְוִי בִינָֽה׃

i18n.en: Who placed wisdom in the inward parts, or who gave understanding to the mind?

paragraphs.commentary: **A contested verse.** Two hapax-style nouns: *tuchot* (טֻחוֹת — *inward parts, hidden interior*; possibly *ibis* — the Egyptian sacred bird associated with wisdom) and *sekhvi* (שֶׂכְוִי — *rooster*, in later Hebrew; here possibly *mind, heart-as-locus-of-thought*). The verse's exact subject is unresolved. // Three readings circulate: (1) **hidden interior** (the seat of human wisdom located in the inward organs); (2) **animal-wisdom** (the verse names two birds — ibis and rooster — as wisdom-instinct examples, consistent with the chapter's animal-catalog in vv 39-41); (3) **clouds-and-meteors** (taking *tuchot* and *sekhvi* as obscure atmospheric phenomena). The chapter does not specify. The translation goes with the inward-parts reading; commentary surfaces the cruces.

paragraphs.text: מִֽי־יְסַפֵּ֣ר שְׁחָקִ֣ים בְּחָכְמָ֑ה וְנִבְלֵ֥י שָׁ֝מַ֗יִם מִ֣י יַשְׁכִּֽיב׃

i18n.en: Who can count the clouds in wisdom, or tip the bottles of the skies,

paragraphs.text: בְּצֶ֣קֶת עָ֭פָר לַמּוּצָ֑ק וּרְגָבִ֥ים יְדֻבָּֽקוּ׃

i18n.en: when the dust pours into hardness and the clods cling together?

paragraphs.commentary: **A drought-and-rain image.** Dust *pours like molten metal* (*la-mutzaq* — *into the molten / poured-thing*); clods *cling together* — the chapter is describing the moisture-cycle that transforms loose dust into clinging earth. The image is **alchemical-procedural**: dry dust becomes wet aggregate becomes solid earth through the rain-cycle.

paragraphs.text: הֲתָצ֣וּד לְלָבִ֣יא טָ֑רֶף וְחַיַּ֖ת כְּפִירִ֣ים תְּמַלֵּֽא׃

i18n.en: Can you hunt prey for the lioness, or fill the appetite of the young lions,

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter pivots to the animal kingdom.** The first divine speech (chs 38-39) divides structurally: vv 4-38 are cosmological-atmospheric; vv 39-41 introduce the animal-world catalog that will run through chapter 39. // *Lavi* (לָבִיא) — *lioness* — names the predatory cat-class; *kfirim* (כְּפִירִים) is *young lions* (lions in their prime). The chapter is asking whether Job can *provide for the predators* — feed the carnivorous food-chain. The implicit framing: the food-chain itself is divinely-managed.

paragraphs.text: כִּי־יָשֹׁ֥חוּ בַמְּעוֹנ֑וֹת יֵשְׁב֖וּ בַסֻּכָּ֣ה לְמוֹ־אָֽרֶב׃

i18n.en: when they crouch in their dens, sit in their lair to lie in ambush?

paragraphs.text: מִ֤י יָכִ֥ין לָעֹרֵ֗ב צֵ֫יד֥וֹ כִּֽי־ילדו [יְ֭לָדָיו] אֶל־אֵ֣ל יְשַׁוֵּ֑עוּ יִ֝תְע֗וּ לִבְלִי־אֹֽכֶל׃

i18n.en: Who prepares prey for the raven when its young cry to El, wander without food?

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter closes on the raven.** *La-orev tzeydo* — *prey for the raven*. The same bird as the one Noah sent out first from the ark in Gen 8:7. The raven is the canonical Hebrew Bible scavenger-bird, often appearing alongside ritually-unclean associations. The chapter is staging the raven's chick-feeding as a divinely-managed function. // *Yeshawe'u* — *cry out* — from *shava* (cry, call for help). The raven-chicks **cry to El** — a striking moment. The chapter is naming animal-prayer / animal-distress-calls as addressed to *El* (the broader-divine class-name, the same root as *Elohim*). The animal world prays; the chapter affirms that the prayers are *heard*. // *Ketiv/qere* note: *yeladav* (qere) for *yldw* (ketiv). The qere is the standard masoretic vocalization. // The chapter ends — chapter 39 will continue the divine speech with an extended catalog of animals (the wild donkey, wild ox, ostrich, horse, hawk, eagle).
